$comment: Per-checker configuration for this repo. Each checker falls back to its own defaults when its key is absent, so deleting a block degrades to the built-in behaviour rather than to an empty scope. What lives here is what changes between repos: layout, thresholds, and the regexes that name one stack's idioms. What stays in code is the rule itself.
$profile: The shape this repo claims to hold, not the tools it uses: baseline = one axis measures · standard = two axes block, both meta-checks present · hardened = every declared axis blocks and every gate job is asserted. A profile is a claim someone else can fail you on, which is the only kind worth writing down.
$baselines: Level 2 means `baseline the old, block the new`, so an axis at 2 must name WHERE its debt is frozen and WHICH direction counts as improvement — otherwise the frozen number is a photograph nobody can compare against. `improves`: down = a per-key number may only decrease · shrink = a set may only lose members · tighten = a status may only move to the stricter value. The direction lives here rather than inside the baseline file because `--update-baseline` rewrites those files, and a rule that a re-freeze can silently drop is not a rule.

$postMerge.$what: The ci.yml jobs that run after the merge instead of before it: on every push to a gated branch, nightly, and on a workflow_dispatch naming the branch the work lands on in its base input, never on a pull request, and absent from ci-passed.needs, so a red one blocks nothing and is fixed forward by whichever run lands next. The dispatch is how a branch that needs one of them — a Windows-only runner fix, say — runs it before it lands. One of them carries a behaviour-axis gate — check-whole-tree-gates --run is whole-tree — while core-integration runs the integration suite, and images and runner-platforms (the macOS and Windows runner legs) belong to no axis. conformance-audit R12 holds this list and ci-passed.needs to one partition of the workflow's jobs.
$postMerge.$costs: The owner ruled on 2026-09-30 that forge-dev, a beta with no production, ships as fast as possible. What is traded: a migration or real-Postgres regression, an image that no longer builds, a whole-repository guard broken by a change outside core, and a runtime difference only macOS or Windows shows (CRLF, path separators, temp-dir symlinks) each reach main green and are found after the merge rather than before it — the shapes that PR #336, fd3230e93 and #710 each once landed through. What is NOT traded: compile and lint errors for all three runner targets still gate the pull request, through the ubuntu runner job's cross-target clippy for x86_64-pc-windows-gnu and x86_64-apple-darwin (owner addition, 2026-10-01, after three of four runner PRs went red on macOS or Windows alone). A pull request touching core stops waiting roughly ten minutes on core-integration.
$postMerge.$ends: When the owner says forge-dev is going to production. Then each job returns to ci-passed.needs and its result loop, its pull_request condition is dropped, and this block is deleted — a revert of ISS-1370's ci.yml change.

$amnesty.$costs: Each may stay over 500 lines (or 150 per function) and grow no further; a reader of these two pays the length, and a third file growing past the budget is still refused.

knowledge.owns: whether a document asking to be adopted prices what adopting it costs; whether the PAT permission menu covers every route it claims; whether one question in the source has more than one answer; whether a document's citations of this repo's own files are still true; whether the committed API and MCP contracts are what the code serves, route by route and tool by tool

relations.owns: which module may depend on which: archmap's contracts, and pattern v2's context direction, kind direction, runtime cycles, face-only access and adapter ports (check-module-boundaries, its shrink-only baseline in .forge/module-boundaries-baseline.json enforced by the checker itself against the base revision); and which module may write which table, where a database call, a refusal and the global fetch may be written (check-module-shape, type-aware ESLint rules ratcheted by the bulk suppressions in .forge/module-shape-suppressions.json, whose per-rule total may not rise over the base revision)

alsoBaseline.$why: archmap lock writes this, and without a direction that command is an amnesty button: run it and today's violations stop blocking. `down` means the frozen TOTAL may not rise and no per-key count may rise, so freezing a new file in fails and letting a blob grow inside its own entry fails, while fixing one and re-freezing is free.

alsoBaseline.$compositionRoots: A declared exemption, not a freeze: packages/core/src/index.ts, route-registry.ts, work-ports.ts, execution-ports.ts, integration-registry.ts, timer-registry.ts and outbox-consumers.ts are in .arch.json's exclude (ISS-225): each is a composition root that wires every module at boot, so its fan-out is its purpose. They are named file by file; any other file is still held to 6.

behaviour.owns: whether a test asserts behaviour or restates a declaration; whether every tracked test file is collected by a runner at all

record.owns: whether the external record of what shipped keeps the heading its readers parse for, whether an entry once published can be removed without saying so, and whether a NEW entry stays inside the word budget a reader can actually read
record.$why: The other five axes each own a property of the CODE. On 2026-08-28 commit 3df9a8e9 removed 1,034 lines from CHANGELOG.md inside a docs-pointer commit whose message never named the file; twelve gates ran and every one passed, because the record was nobody's. No baseline: it starts at zero debt, and a removal is declared per-instance in .forge/changelog-amnesty.json rather than frozen in bulk — a public record is edited one line at a time or not at all. Budget added 2026-09-16 (ENTRY_WORD_BUDGET, 40): unbounded, the record reached 443 entries and 86,206 words with a median of 173 — the second failure mode, opposite the raw-commit dump, where the detail is present but not findable. It measures only entries a change ADDS, for the same reason there is no baseline: the entries already published are rewritten one at a time, not frozen by declaring them once.

archmap.$comment: Ceiling on edges `arch check` cannot resolve. Measured 2026-08-23: 171, all of them node_modules subpath exports (hono/http-exception and friends), which belong to no module and so cannot violate a contract. It was 997 until `.arch.json` declared a tsConfig — 841 of those were web-v2's `@/*` alias, and an unresolvable edge is DROPPED, so three locked contracts over that package were being checked against an empty graph. It had drifted back to 201 by 2026-09-16, 167 of them `hono/http-exception`; a `hono/*` entry in `.arch-tsconfig.json` took it to 33 with `archmap check` still reporting 0 blocking and the same 10 frozen, so nothing was being hidden by the drop. The ceiling came down 200 -> 50 in the same change (ISS-1046): a ceiling four times the measurement is not a ratchet. What remains is the MCP SDK's subpath exports and mermaid. Audit rule R7 fails if it climbs back.

status-tuples.$comment: ISS-1106 — one question, one answer, and one name answers one question. Two constants holding the same status tuple are one answer with two labels, and an inline copy is a third label with no name at all; each is a place a later change can move one copy and leave the rest. The vocabularies are read out of their machines in `packages/contracts/src` (`issue-machine.ts`, `job-machine.ts`, `session-machine.ts`) rather than listed here, so a rename there stops the scan instead of quietly narrowing it. `packages/web-v2/src` is scanned beside core and contracts, and literals are read in either quote style because web-v2 is formatted with double quotes. A `Record<…Status, boolean>` is a declaration of its `true` keys; a `Record<…Status, T>` for any other T is a lookup table and stays unread. A pair that must differ is admitted by a `status-tuple: differs — <reason>` comment at the declaration, and that marker excuses a declaration only against a peer it names. A name holding two different tuples is refused whatever the markers say. What it deliberately does not read: SQL string literals, type unions, and a tuple written as an object-literal value, which is a table row rather than a named question. In a test file only `.each` case lists are read, because that list is the domain a test claims to cover. The limit: a gate that keys a tuple by its members catches a second copy before it drifts, never one that already has. `run-machine.ts:PIPELINE_RUN_STATUSES` is not one of the vocabularies read; that residual is docs/proposals/status-tuple-residuals.md.

doc-citations.$comment: ISS-1112 — a document that names a file makes a claim a machine can check, and nothing checked it: 93 documents had drifted far enough to be deleted rather than corrected before this landed, one of them crediting an invariant to a test file not in the tree. The unit is a CITATION, never a document — prose is not checkable and this does not try. A citation is resolved in two scopes and no third — the document's own directory and the package the document sits in — with a path written from the repository root resolved exactly or not at all. Nothing falls back to the whole tree, and no part of resolution reads whether the target is present: a resolution that widens at the moment a file disappears is a resolution that cannot report the disappearance. The cost is real and is paid rather than hidden: a document at the repository root writes the full path or is told it cites nothing, which is what the sweep in ISS-1112 did to sixteen citations in `CLAUDE.md` and `scripts/README.md`. One residual is stated at `scripts/check-doc-citations.mjs` rather than left to be found: a document inside a scope citing a root-level file whose name is ALSO taken inside that scope resolves to the root copy while it exists and to the scoped namesake once it is deleted. Closing it takes a syntactic root notation and a rewrite of every rooted citation in the repository. Nothing detects the collision while both files exist either, because the exact match returns before any scoped candidate is looked for; what bounds it is only that it needs one name taken twice, at the root and inside the citing document's own scope, which this repository does not do today. Three shapes fail: a path no tracked file carries, a line-number citation (which CLAUDE.md already forbids by name), and a file.ts:symbol anchor whose file does not hold that symbol. One shape only reports: a citation whose target was changed after the document was, which is the still-true/edited/deleted worklist entry and not a build failure. What it cannot see, each stated where it is skipped: prose, fenced and indented code blocks, a path in another repository (which carries no extension here and so is not read as a citation at all), a symbol that still exists but has changed meaning, and whether a count or a number in a document is right. A token that is not a claim about this repository says so at the citation, in an HTML comment reading `doc-citation: unchecked `<token>` `<token>` — <why>`, which NAMES what it excuses: a window alone would reach every citation in the same paragraph, and the migration README's template marker sat three lines above a live `meta/_journal.json` it would then have hidden. A marker naming no token is refused rather than left to excuse nothing in silence. Resolution reads the working tree as well as the index, because `git ls-files` still lists a file deleted and not yet staged — which is the one run whose job is to notice it went.

skipDocs.why: The external record of what shipped. It records what was true on the day it shipped and is MEANT to age — a citation in a released entry going stale is the record working, not rotting. Named out of scope by ISS-1112 and owned by the `record` axis instead.

A proposal names the tree it WANTS, not the tree there is, so a forward reference and a dead citation are the same text and this checker cannot tell them apart. `check-honest-costs` already owns these documents on the axis they can be measured on: whether they price what adopting them costs.
A vendored third-party plugin's own documents, shipped with its source. Its citations are about its own tree and land here only because `pnpm install` needs no path outside the repo.
The same: `eslint-plugin-code-quality` vendored at a path inside the repo so installation needs no path outside it. Its documents are its author's.

Snapshots kept for recovery. A citation in a backup describes the tree AT THE TIME IT WAS TAKEN, which is the whole point of keeping it, so measuring it against today's tree would report the backup working as a fault.

provider-literals.$comment: ISS-1071 — an integration provider's name is written in the places that describe a provider, and nowhere else. The rule is about LOCATION, not about the value: `IntegrationProvider` makes 'coolify' legal everywhere the union is in scope, which is what a union is for, so no type can hold this and the check has to be a scan. What it matches, and the two bounds it carries, are stated at the top of scripts/lib/provider-literals.mjs.

unscannable.why: 'agent' is a provider name AND this repo's word for an actor, an author, a principal and a conversation participant — `kind: 'agent'`, `author: 'agent'`, `role: 'agent'`. Measured 2026-09-17 across the three scan roots: 81 files write the bare literal and at most six of them are about the integration, so including it would run the checker at over 90% noise, which is the one failure a checker cannot recover from — a reader who learns to skip the report also skips the real finding underneath it. What holds `agent` instead is the type (it is a member of IntegrationProvider, so a wrong use in an integration position is a compile error). Retire this entry when the actor vocabulary stops sharing the word, not before; the checker prints it on every run so the exclusion cannot go quiet.

allowed.why: The provider's own directory — the one place ISS-1071 puts a provider's name. Everything here is ABOUT coolify and no generic path reads it.
The provider's own directory — the one place ISS-1071 puts a provider's name. Everything here is ABOUT epodsystem and no generic path reads it.
The provider's own directory — the one place ISS-1071 puts a provider's name. Everything here is ABOUT autoflow and no generic path reads it.

The codec between a binding-v1 target and its integration_bindings row: it switches exhaustively on the same per-provider union schema.ts declares (a coolify applicationUuid onto the targets[] its deploy adapter reads, a shopify store onto the binding config, epodsystem refused by name), so each arm names the provider whose row shape it writes. A provider added to the union is a compile error here, not a silent default.

The schema vocabulary of the project-config v1 documents: each binding target is one provider's own shape (a coolify applicationUuid, a shopify or epodsystem store), so the discriminated union has to name the provider it describes, and the storefront and deployment-record enums are the providers the published JSON Schema admits, which is narrower than the registry by design. Deriving them from the registry would widen the published contract silently whenever a provider is added.
The provider's own directory — the one place ISS-1071 puts a provider's name. Everything here is ABOUT sentry and no generic path reads it.
The provider's own directory — the one place ISS-1071 puts a provider's name. Everything here is ABOUT rocketchat and no generic path reads it.
The provider's own directory — the one place ISS-1071 puts a provider's name. Everything here is ABOUT github and no generic path reads it.
The provider's own directory — the one place ISS-1071 puts a provider's name. Everything here is ABOUT gitlab and no generic path reads it (ISS-50).
The registry itself. Every generic path asks a question here instead of naming a provider, which is precisely what makes this the file the names arrive in.

The `IntegrationProvider` union and `INTEGRATION_PROVIDERS` beside it are the vocabulary. The checker reads its own scanned set out of this file, so forbidding the names here would forbid the list it works from.

The database schema's own vocabulary. A column declared `{ enum: [...] }` stores these strings and rows already written carry them, so a name here is on disk in every deployment rather than a branch in code — `schema-conversations.ts` and `schema-rocketchat.ts` also name a provider in a TABLE name, which no refactor can reach without a migration.

The cross-package contract surface web-v2 reads. Core's production image does not carry contracts, so a runtime value cannot cross from core to here; where a provider name has to be legible on the web side it is written in contracts.
`DEPLOY_CAPABLE_PROVIDERS` — the list deliberately mirrored across the package boundary, because neither package may import a runtime value from the other.

The web side's per-provider modules — the browser mirror of a provider's own directory. `providers/<provider>/section.tsx` is ABOUT that provider and no generic screen reads it; what is left in features/integrations/components and in derive.ts is generic and still reported.

`github` and `google` here are LOGIN identity providers — a different namespace that happens to share two words with the integration vocabulary. `providers.ts` answers /api/auth/oauth/providers, which never touches an integration binding, so a registry lookup here would be the wrong answer rather than a tidier one.

The identity port (ADR 0006): the GitHub OAuth and OIDC login providers auth/oauth signs people in through. `github` and `google` here are the same LOGIN identity namespace as auth/oauth, not integration-provider names, and nothing here touches an integration binding.

The browser half of the same login-identity namespace: the sign-in buttons and the token screens read `github`/`google` as OAuth providers, which is a different thing from an integration adapter that happens to share the word.

The `ConversationAdapter` union: which surface a conversation happened on. It mirrors the `conversations.source` column, not `integration_bindings.provider`, and it carries 'web' and 'widget' which are not integrations at all.

The one hand-built card, keyed 'github', is derived from `projects.repoUrl` and NOT from any integration binding — which is exactly why `githubIntegration` declares `presentation: null`, so the registry loop cannot emit a second card that collides with it. Every other card in this file comes from a declaration.

The `forge_storefront_target` MCP tool, living in the integration door and reading the registry through the integrations port face. It answers only about the storefront providers (epodsystem, autoflow) and names them in the description a model reads; no other provider's request reaches it.

The integration door's per-provider route modules (ISS-167): `coolify-routes.ts` and `github-connect-routes.ts` are each ABOUT the provider they are named for, mounted by the route registry and read by no generic path. They left the provider directories because an adapter holds no HTTP door; the name came with them.

The Coolify release commands, controls, confirmation and health gate (ISS-167), named for the provider because each is that provider's deploy as the release drives it, beside `release-coolify.ts`, which names the provider only through its adapter's declaration. They moved out of the adapter because what a deploy means to a run is the release's; nothing generic reads them to learn a provider exists.

The error-intake slice (ISS-167) turns an error tracker's sightings into issues. `sentry` here is the `issues.source` value and the `issues.metadata` key rows already written carry, so the name is on disk rather than a branch in code; the vendor itself is reached only through `integrations/sentry`.

The pull-request projection, moved from `integrations/github/` into the source-host port (ISS-167). A stored change request written before hosts were recorded is a GitHub one, so `github` is the default it reads such a row back under.
The projection's health read, moved from `integrations/github/` with it (ISS-167). The webhook-fed projection exists only for a GitHub binding, so the query names the provider whose bindings feed it.

The deploy port's record contract (ISS-167, from `project-config/deploy-adapters/types.ts`): the provider union is the one the recorded environment state stores, mirrored here so the adapter side owns its contract without importing the domain's schema.

The assistant's chat-room door (ISS-167, split out of `integrations/rocketchat/`): the escalation and agent-chat bridges, the question and comment lanes of a Rocket.Chat room, and its conversation ports, window drain and turn inputs (moved from `conversations/chat-room/` by ISS-203). `rocketchat` here is the `conversations.source` and question-origin `adapter` value rows already carry, and the provider a room binding is looked up under; the vendor itself is reached only through the `integrations/rocketchat` port.

egress.$comment: ADR 0006: every external system is reached through one adapter under integrations/<port>/. A vendor SDK import anywhere else in core is refused by file and line. The rule is about LOCATION, as the provider-literal rule beside it is, so it rides the same scan. The global fetch is the module-shape lint's (scripts/eslint-module-shape/rules/global-fetch.mjs), whose allow list carries its own reasons.

exceptions.why: Forge's own crash reporting, initialised at boot before any domain module loads, and the one module that imports @sentry/node. Callers reach it through its role-typed functions (reportFailure, reportCondition, traceStep, flushReports) and never name the vendor's namespace.

integration-declarations.$comment: ISS-1071 — the registry is only a single door while every declaration behind it answers the questions the generic paths ask. A missing field does not fail to compile once a declaration reaches the registry through a widened type, and the reader then sees a provider that is inert rather than one that did not answer; five of seven adapters reached the old registry through `as any`. This walks the LIVE registry rather than the source, so the thing measured is what the process would hold at boot. `entrypoint` is imported under tsx with a synthetic env; its absence is exit 2, never a pass over an empty registry.

lint-budget.$comment: Registering a class is this list plus one `--update-baseline` run — no second script, no second baseline file. That is the whole claim ISS-833 made for a shared ratchet, and `packages/core` is the proof of it: its `warn`-severity rules produced 280 diagnostics that nothing counted, because biome exits 0 on a warning. A scope with no `drain` block is freeze-only.
lint-budget.$drain: Freezing does not reduce — an earlier comment baseline sat frozen for months at 3% drained. `drain` adds the rule that does: a file in the branch delta matching `include` and not `exclude`, whose baseline count is above zero, must come back STRICTLY lower. web-v2 declares none on purpose: 98 debt-carrying files with the formatter deliberately off is a separate decision from turning the linter on.
